title: MARRIAGE WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO MAKE ATTRACTION DISAPPEAR
paragraphs:
MARRIAGE WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO MAKE ATTRACTION DISAPPEAR
You can love your spouse, love Jesus, and still notice that someone else is attractive. The question that reveals your heart is not whether your eyes noticed—but what you allowed your heart to do next.
There are some struggles Christians confess easily.
“I’ve been anxious.”
“I’ve been angry.”
“I haven’t prayed like I should.”
But there are other struggles we bury beneath church clothes, wedding rings, family photographs, anniversary posts, and carefully rehearsed smiles.
Because saying them aloud feels dangerous.
So let’s say one of them.
You got married.
You meant your vows.
You love your spouse.
You have no intention of destroying your marriage.
And then one ordinary day, someone walked into the room...
and you noticed.
They were attractive.
Maybe very attractive.
And for one uncomfortable second, something inside you woke up that you thought marriage was supposed to switch off forever.
Then came the guilt.
Why did I notice?
What is wrong with me?
Does this mean I don’t really love my spouse?
Does this mean something is missing in my marriage?
Am I already being unfaithful?
Or perhaps your reaction went in the opposite direction.
I’m married, not blind.
Looking doesn’t hurt anybody.
It’s just attraction.
And somewhere between unnecessary shame and dangerous self-justification is a truth many Christians desperately need to understand:
Marriage was never supposed to make attraction disappear.
Marriage was supposed to teach us what covenant does with desire.
That distinction matters.
Because Scripture does not teach that the wedding ceremony removes your capacity to recognize beauty.
It teaches something far deeper.
Your desires no longer get to be your master.
Jesus does.
And that changes everything.
The Bible begins the story of marriage with breathtaking intimacy.
Genesis 2:24 says that a man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become “בָּשָׂר אֶחָד” — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people sharing a house.
Not merely two people legally attached to one another.
One flesh.
Covenant intimacy.
A joining of lives.
Then Scripture gives us one of the most vulnerable descriptions of human intimacy in the entire Bible:
“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים... וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
That was the original picture.
Desire without exploitation.
Nakedness without manipulation.
Intimacy without comparison.
Love without hiding.
Then sin entered.
And almost immediately...
they hid.
That is worth remembering.
Sin did not invent beauty.
Sin distorted what we do with beauty.
Sin did not invent desire.
Sin corrupted desire.
And the Gospel is not God's plan to turn human beings into emotionless creatures who can no longer recognize attractiveness.
The Gospel transforms what rules us.
That is why marriage cannot be reduced to the expectation that your spouse will become the only physically attractive human being you can perceive.
That expectation may sound spiritual.
It isn't biblical.
Your wedding ring did not rewire your optic nerves.
Your vows did something much more serious.
They established covenant boundaries around what you will pursue.
There is an enormous difference between seeing beauty...
and feeding desire.
Between noticing...
and nurturing.
Between experiencing temptation...
and entertaining it.
Between an involuntary moment of recognition...
and the second look you deliberately take because you want more.
That is where many marriages begin bleeding long before anybody touches anybody.
Jesus went directly to the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, He warned about looking at another person πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai.
The language matters.
Jesus was not teaching that the mere biological recognition that another human being is attractive automatically constitutes adultery.
His warning penetrates much deeper: the gaze can become intentional, possessive, cultivated desire.
The issue is not simply that your eyes registered beauty.
The issue is what your heart decided to do with what your eyes saw.
That is uncomfortable.
Because adultery does not always begin in a bedroom.
Sometimes it begins in imagination.
Sometimes with a conversation you secretly hope will continue.
Sometimes with a notification that makes your heart beat differently.
Sometimes with deleting messages.
Sometimes with comparing your spouse to somebody who has never had to carry real life with you.
Sometimes with looking at another person's carefully curated photographs while forgetting the exhausted, faithful human being sleeping beside you.
Sometimes nothing “happened.”
But something has already been happening.
Inside you.
And Jesus cares about that hidden room.
Not because He wants to humiliate you.
Because He loves you too much to let secret desire quietly become your master.
James describes temptation with frightening clarity:
“Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.”
Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin.
Notice the progression.
Desire can be entertained.
Fed.
Carried.
Conceived.
And eventually something hidden becomes something destructive.
This is why temptation itself must not be confused with surrender to temptation.
Jesus Himself “has been tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
So experiencing temptation cannot itself automatically equal sin, because our sinless Savior was genuinely tempted.
That truth can free someone reading this from crushing, unnecessary shame.
You noticed someone attractive?
That moment does not automatically mean your marriage is fake.
You experienced temptation?
That does not automatically mean you betrayed your spouse.
But what happens next matters.
A lot.
Because temptation is not permission.
And grace is not permission either.
Maybe nobody has ever explained this to you.
You don't necessarily need to panic because someone caught your attention.
You need to guard what receives your attention afterward.
You don't have to pretend beautiful people suddenly stopped existing when you exchanged vows.
You have to remember that beauty does not give you ownership.
Attraction does not give you permission.
Chemistry does not cancel covenant.
Opportunity does not equal God's approval.
And dissatisfaction at home does not transform temptation into destiny.
Read that again.
Because someone is eventually going to appear who seems easier than your spouse.
They won't carry the history of your arguments.
They won't remind you about bills.
They won't have years of unresolved misunderstandings attached to their voice.
You may only see them when they are dressed well, smiling, attentive, energetic, interested.
Meanwhile, you see your spouse tired.
Stressed.
Sick.
Irritated.
Unshaven.
Without makeup.
Worried about money.
Cleaning up after children.
Recovering from childbirth.
Working overtime.
Growing older.
Carrying grief.
Trying to survive.
And suddenly comparison commits fraud against your marriage.
Because you compare somebody else's presentation...
with your spouse's entire humanity.
You compare a stranger's highlight reel with your covenant partner's behind-the-scenes footage.
Of course fantasy feels lighter.
Fantasy has never had to pay a mortgage with you.
Fantasy has never awakened beside you at 3:17 in the morning because the baby was screaming.
Fantasy has never seen you sick.
Fantasy has never had to forgive your sharp words.
Fantasy has never watched your body change.
Fantasy has never discovered your weaknesses and chosen to remain.
Fantasy has never carried your history.
Your spouse has.
And perhaps the most dangerous attraction is not always physical.
Sometimes what seduces the heart is being understood.
Someone listens.
Someone laughs.
Someone notices you.
Someone says the thing you wish your spouse would say.
And slowly, almost innocently, you begin giving someone else pieces of yourself that should have been protected.
You tell yourself:
We're just friends.
Maybe you are.
But ask yourself the question people usually avoid:
Would you communicate exactly the same way if your spouse were sitting beside you reading every word?
Would you want your husband to hear that conversation?
Would you want your wife to see those messages?
Would you feel the need to explain why you deleted anything?
If secrecy is required to preserve the relationship...
something is already wrong.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Above all else, guard your heart.”
The Hebrew word often translated “heart” is לֵב — lev.
In biblical thought, the heart is not merely the emotional part of a person. It reaches into the inner life—the place of thought, intention, desire, and decision.
Guard it.
Not because every person outside your marriage is dangerous.
Because an unguarded heart can make dangerous things out of ordinary encounters.
And please hear this:
Guarding your marriage does not mean treating every attractive person as an enemy.
It means refusing to make them an escape.
It means refusing to secretly rehearse a life with someone God has not given you.
It means refusing to nourish fantasies that slowly make covenant faithfulness feel boring.
It means refusing to use pornography as a substitute for intimacy.
It means refusing to turn social media into a private catalog of bodies.
It means refusing emotional affairs simply because nobody has kissed yet.
It means refusing to call something innocent merely because it has not become physical.
Job expressed radical intentionality when he said:
“I have made a covenant with my eyes.”
A covenant with his eyes.
Imagine that.
Not hatred of beauty.
Not fear of humanity.
Discipline.
Because mature faithfulness is not pretending temptation doesn't exist.
It is deciding beforehand what you will do when it arrives.
Joseph did not stand in Potiphar's house negotiating with temptation.
He ran.
Sometimes the holiest thing you can do is leave.
Close the conversation.
Unfollow the account.
Delete the number.
Change the routine.
Tell your spouse the truth.
Call a mature believer.
Confess.
Get accountability.
Stop going somewhere you know repeatedly weakens you.
Not because running makes you weak.
Sometimes running proves you finally understand how weak you can become.
Paul told Timothy:
“Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace.”
Notice that Christianity is not merely run away.
It is also run toward.
Run toward righteousness.
Run toward faith.
Run toward love.
Run toward peace.
Run toward Christ.
And if you are married...
run toward your spouse again.
Because sometimes the answer to attraction outside marriage is not merely starving something outside.
It is rebuilding something inside.
When did you stop dating each other?
When did every conversation become logistics?
When did “How was your day?” become the deepest question you asked?
When did affection become something expected instead of something intentionally given?
When did you stop flirting with the person you married?
When did you stop telling them they were beautiful?
When did you stop touching without demanding sex?
When did you stop laughing?
When did the phones become more interesting than the person sitting three feet away?
When did resentment begin sleeping between you?
Maybe attraction did not disappear.
Maybe attention did.
And attention can often be reclaimed.
Song of Songs destroys the idea that biblical marriage must be emotionally sterile or embarrassed by marital desire.
Scripture contains celebration of attraction within covenant.
Husband and wife delight in one another.
They speak beauty.
They express longing.
They enjoy each other.
God is not embarrassed by marital desire.
He designed covenant intimacy.
Christian holiness is not the murder of desire.
It is desire brought under the lordship of Christ and directed according to God's wisdom.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 7 about mutual marital responsibility and intimacy. Ephesians 5 goes deeper still, presenting marriage through the astonishing mystery of Christ and His Church.
Marriage ultimately points beyond itself.
Your spouse was never meant to become your savior.
That burden would crush them.
Your husband cannot complete what only Christ can redeem.
Your wife cannot heal every wound only Christ can reach.
No human being can permanently satisfy the deepest hunger of a soul created for God.
And this is where some marriages quietly go wrong.
We demand from another human being what only Jesus can provide.
Then when they inevitably fail, someone new looks like salvation.
They aren't.
They're human too.
Give fantasy enough time and it eventually becomes ordinary life.
The person who seems flawless from a distance also has wounds, habits, insecurities, selfishness, mornings, moods, weaknesses, and sins.
You are not comparing two realities.
You are comparing reality with imagination.
Reality almost always loses that competition.
So perhaps the question is not:
“Why am I attracted to somebody else?”
Maybe the deeper questions are:
“What am I doing with that attraction?”
“What hunger is this exposing?”
“What boundary needs strengthening?”
“What conversation have I been avoiding?”
“What resentment have I been feeding?”
“What part of my marriage needs attention?”
“What part of my own soul needs repentance?”
And ultimately:
“Is Jesus Lord here too?”
Not just Lord of Sunday.
Not just Lord of theology.
Not just Lord of the Bible verses you post.
Lord of your eyes.
Lord of your imagination.
Lord of your private messages.
Lord of your browser history.
Lord of your loneliness.
Lord of your sexuality.
Lord of the fantasies nobody knows about.
Lord of the part of you that wants to be wanted.
That is where discipleship becomes real.
Maybe this article found you after you already crossed a line.
Maybe yours is not theoretical.
Maybe there is a name attached to this.
A conversation.
A hotel room.
A photograph.
A secret account.
Pornography.
An emotional affair.
An actual affair.
Maybe your spouse still doesn't know.
And you have been carrying the terrifying thought:
If people knew what I did, they would never look at me the same way again.
Perhaps they wouldn't.
Sin has consequences.
Trust can be shattered.
Families can be wounded.
Repentance does not magically remove every earthly consequence of what we have done.
The Gospel never requires us to pretend sin isn't serious.
The cross proves precisely how serious sin is.
But the cross also tells us something else.
Your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Look at Jesus.
Look at the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Dragged into public shame.
Reduced to her worst moment.
Surrounded by people holding stones.
Her sin mattered.
But Jesus refused to let condemnation have the final word.
“Neither do I condemn you,” He told her.
And then:
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Grace...
and transformation.
Mercy...
and repentance.
Jesus did not say, “It doesn't matter.”
He essentially gave her something infinitely greater:
Your sin does not have to own your future.
That is Gospel grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not renaming sin.
Not excusing betrayal.
Not hiding consequences.
Grace walks straight into the wreckage and says:
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you have been unfaithful.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out your intimacy.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you have been emotionally attached to someone who isn't your spouse.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you have compared your husband to another man until resentment poisoned your respect.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you have compared your wife's body to women on a screen until you stopped seeing the woman who has faithfully loved you.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you haven't crossed the physical line...
but you know exactly where your imagination has been living.
Jesus can still write from here.
But grace does not say:
“Keep hiding.”
Grace calls you into the light.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
The Greek word translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō—to confess, acknowledge, say the same thing.
Repentance stops negotiating with God about what sin should be called.
It agrees with Him.
No more:
It wasn't technically cheating.
No more:
Everybody does it.
No more:
My spouse drove me to it.
No more:
It was only pornography.
No more:
We were just talking.
No more:
God understands.
Yes.
God understands more completely than anyone.
And because He understands, He knows exactly where the chains are.
Bring them into the light.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia carries the idea of repentance—a decisive change of mind and turning.
Biblical repentance produces movement.
Away from sin.
Toward Christ.
You don't earn forgiveness by becoming clean enough.
You come to Jesus because you cannot clean yourself.
At the cross, Christ carried sin's judgment.
In His resurrection, death did not get the final word.
And when a sinner turns to Christ in faith, forgiveness is not a motivational slogan.
It was purchased at a cost we could never pay.
Maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needed tonight.
Not permission to continue.
Permission to come home.
Come home.
Before the conversation becomes an affair.
Come home.
Before pornography teaches you to despise covenant intimacy.
Come home.
Before secrecy becomes a second life.
Come home.
Before resentment convinces you that betrayal is justified.
And if the damage has already happened...
come home anyway.
Not to easy consequences.
Not necessarily to immediate restoration of trust.
But to Jesus.
Because He still receives repentant sinners.
And if your spouse is the one who betrayed you, please hear this too.
Their sin is not evidence that you were insufficient as a human being.
You do not have to compete with fantasy.
You do not have to transform yourself into every person your spouse might possibly find attractive.
Healing may require truth, boundaries, wise pastoral care, professional counseling, accountability, time, and consequences.
Forgiveness and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
Reconciliation cannot be built on continuing deception.
Truth matters.
Safety matters.
Repentance bears fruit.
And Jesus does not require wounded people to call darkness light in order to prove they understand grace.
But even betrayal does not have to dictate the rest of your existence.
Christ can meet you in the rubble too.
This is why the Gospel is so much bigger than marriage advice.
We do not simply need stronger willpower.
We need transformed hearts.
We need Jesus.
The One who looked at sinners without exploiting them.
The One who touched the rejected without using them.
The One who confronted sin without becoming cruel.
The One who offered grace without compromising truth.
The One who remained faithful all the way to the cross.
Marriage will never make every other attractive person disappear.
But Jesus can teach you a kind of faithfulness stronger than attraction.
A faithfulness that says:
I noticed, but I will not feed it.
I was tempted, but temptation will not become my master.
My marriage is struggling, but betrayal will not become my medicine.
I am lonely, but secrecy will not become my refuge.
I have sinned, but shame will not keep me from Christ.
I have fallen, but by the grace of God, I will not build a home where I fell.
Maybe tonight you need to look at your spouse differently.
Not as the person who failed to remain eternally twenty-five.
Not as the person responsible for fulfilling every emotional need.
Not as the obstacle between you and some imagined better life.
Look at them as a human being entrusted to your covenant love.
Look at those changing eyes.
Those wrinkles.
Those tired hands.
That body that time has touched.
Remember what those hands have carried.
Remember what those eyes have cried over.
Remember the prayers.
Remember the hospital rooms.
Remember the rent.
Remember the children.
Remember the losses.
Remember the ordinary Tuesdays when they stayed.
Remember the person behind the imperfections.
And perhaps tonight...
choose them again.
Not because nobody else is attractive.
Because covenant love is bigger than attraction.
Attraction can happen in a moment.
Covenant is chosen across a lifetime.
And when covenant becomes difficult, remember that Christian marriage was never ultimately designed to proclaim:
“Look how perfect these two people are.”
It was meant to point toward something greater:
Look how faithful Christ is.
Be honest.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
Sometimes three honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer:
I am not the only one fighting.
Not because you need another saved post you never open again.
Someone may be one message away from crossing a boundary.
Someone may already have crossed it and believes Jesus wants nothing more to do with them.
Someone may be drowning in shame.
Someone may need to discover tonight that repentance still has a door...
and His name is Jesus.
Even send it privately to the person you know would never admit publicly that they needed it.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus.
It doesn't.
The grace of God cannot be purchased, and the Gospel is not for sale.

But when Christ has blessed us, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way we voluntarily participate in helping biblical truth reach people who desperately need it. If you want to glorify God through your support, do it with the right heart: not purchasing spiritual favor, but helping the message of Christ travel farther.
And don't keep Gospel Warrior to yourself.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the person who has drifted.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the skeptic.
Even invite the unbeliever who is willing to listen.
Not for an algorithm alone.
For a soul.
Because somewhere behind a smiling profile picture may be a marriage nobody knows is collapsing.
Somewhere behind a church pew may be a believer secretly losing a war with lust.
Somewhere behind an anniversary photograph may be a spouse wondering whether covenant is still worth fighting for.
And somewhere behind a locked screen may be someone whispering:
Have I gone too far for Jesus to want me back?
Tell them.
No.
The cross is still standing.
The tomb is still empty.
Grace is still calling sinners home.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories people thought were already ruined.
Attraction may knock at the door—but it does not have to become the author of your story. Give the pen back to Jesus.
